tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in messages from the system in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use the default 5-minute Anthropic prompt-cache TTL. Sleeping past 300 seconds means the next wake-up reads your full conversation context uncached — slower and more expensive. So the natural breakpoints:

- **Under 5 minutes (60s–270s)**: cache stays warm. Right for actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about — a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue.
- **5 minutes to 1 hour (300s–3600s)**: pay the cache miss. Right when there's no point checking sooner — waiting on something that takes minutes to change, genuinely idle, or as the long fallback heartbeat when something else is the primary wake signal.

**Don't pick 300s.** It's the worst-of-both: you pay the cache miss without amortizing it. If you're tempted to "wait 5 minutes," either drop to 270s (stay in cache) or commit to 1200s+ (one cache miss buys a much longer wait). Don't think in round-number minutes — think in cache windows.

For idle ticks with no specific signal to watch, default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop checks back, you don't burn cache 12× per hour for nothing, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Think about what you're actually waiting for, not just "how long should I sleep." If you're polling a CI run that takes ~8 minutes, sleeping 60s burns the cache 8 times before it finishes — sleep ~270s twice instead.

The runtime clamps to [60, 3600], so you don't need to clamp yourself.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a message from the system confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a message from the system confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

1	# u2-l3 PDF 渲染：从页面坐标到 base64 PNG
2	
3	## 1. 本讲目标
4	
5	学完本讲，你应该能够：
6	
7	1. 解释 PDF 的「点」（point）坐标系与 MediaBox 的含义，并会用 `pdfinfo` 读出任意页面的物理尺寸。
8	2. 推导 `render_pdf_to_base64png` 中 `target_longest_image_dim * 72 / longest_dim` 这个分辨率换算公式，理解「72 像素/点」这一 PDF 坐标约定的来历。
9	3. 独立完成一个渲染实验：对同一个 PDF 页面分别以 644 和 1288 的目标最长边渲染，验证输出 PNG 的最长边确实等于设定值。
10	4. 读懂 `get_png_dimensions_from_base64` 的技巧——不解码整张图片、只切 base64 字符串的前 32 个字符就能读出宽高。
11	
12	本讲在整条流水线中的位置：上一讲（u2-l2）讲的是「输入怎么收进来、怎么分组入队」；worker 从队列取到 PDF 之后、把它发给模型之前，必须先把某一**页**变成一张**图片**——这件事就发生在本讲的 `renderpdf.py` 里。可以说，这是 VLM OCR 的物理起点：**模型看到的从来不是 PDF，而是这一步渲染出来的 PNG**。
13	
14	## 2. 前置知识
15	
16	### 2.1 PDF 的坐标系：点（point）与 MediaBox
17	
18	PDF 是矢量格式，页面本身没有「像素」概念，只有**点**（point/pt）：
19	
20	- 1 点 = 1/72 英寸。这是 1980 年代印刷业沿用下来的约定，也是本讲那个 `72` 的唯一出处。
21	- 每一页用一个 **MediaBox** 矩形描述大小，形式是四个坐标 \([x_0,\ y_0,\ x_1,\ y_1]\)，即左下角 \((x_0, y_0)\) 与右上角 \((x_1, y_1)\)。
22	- 最常见的美国信纸（Letter）页面是 8.5×11 英寸，换算成点就是 \(8.5 \times 72 = 612\)、\(11 \times 72 = 792\)，所以你会到处看到 `612 x 792` 这个数字（本仓库 `tests/gnarly_pdfs/edgar.pdf` 第一页就是它，`tests/test_anchor.py` 的断言里印着 `Page dimensions: 612.0x792.0`）。
23	- 注意 MediaBox 的原点**不必**是 (0, 0)——坐标可以整体平移，理论上甚至可以方向相反。这就是为什么源码里算宽高要取差值的绝对值。
24	
25	### 2.2 位图与 DPI：像素是怎么来的
26	
27	把矢量页面变成位图（光栅化）时，需要一个**分辨率**（DPI，每英寸像素数）。换算关系是：
28	
29	\[ \text{像素数} = \text{点数} \times \frac{\text{dpi}}{72} \]
30	
31	例如 612 点宽的页面在 150 DPI 下渲染，宽度就是 \(612 \times 150 / 72 = 1275\) 像素。**同一个 PDF，DPI 不同，出来的图大小完全不同**——这是本讲要精读的核心机制。
32	
33	### 2.3 base64 与 data URL
34	
35	`base64` 把任意二进制编码成纯 ASCII 文本（3 字节 → 4 字符）。之所以必须编码，是因为渲染出的 PNG 要塞进发给推理服务的 **JSON 请求体**里，形如 `data:image/png;base64,xxxx...`，JSON 不能直接装原始二进制。
36	
37	### 2.4 PNG 文件的开头长什么样
38	
39	PNG 文件有固定的头部结构，本讲第三个模块就建立在这上面：
40	
41	| 偏移（字节） | 长度 | 内容 |
42	|---|---|---|
43	| 0–7 | 8 | 文件签名 `\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n` |
44	| 8–11 | 4 | 第一个 chunk 的长度（IHDR 恒为 13） |
45	| 12–15 | 4 | chunk 类型，恒为 ASCII `IHDR` |
46	| **16–19** | 4 | **宽度**（大端整数） |
47	| **20–23** | 4 | **高度**（大端整数） |
48	| 24 起 | … | 位深、颜色类型等，本讲用不到 |
49	
50	也就是说：**想知道一张 PNG 的尺寸，只需要文件的第 16~24 字节**。一张 1288 像素页面的 PNG 可能有几百 KB，但读尺寸只需要 9 个字节——`get_png_dimensions_from_base64` 的全部聪明之处就在于此。
51	
52	### 2.5 你需要的环境
53	
54	本讲的实践只需要第 1 单元装好的**轻量环境**：`pip install olmocr` + 系统级的 poppler（`pdfinfo`、`pdftoppm` 两个命令）+ Pillow。不需要 GPU，不需要模型。

146	### 4.2 渲染单页：`render_pdf_to_base64png` 与 72 像素/点
147	
148	#### 4.2.1 概念说明
149	
150	知道页面有多少点之后，就能算出「要让最长边恰好是 D 像素，该用多少 DPI」。核心是一句话：**像素数 = 点数 × dpi / 72**（72 像素/点正是 DPI 定义与 PDF 点定义的换算桥）。
151	
152	设页面最长边为 \(L\) 点、目标最长边为 \(D\) 像素，解方程 \(L \times \text{dpi} / 72 = D\) 得：
153	
154	\[ \text{dpi} = \frac{D \times 72}{L} \]
155	
156	这正是源码第 52 行那个表达式。这样渲染出的图**最长边精确等于 D**（像素取整可能有 ±1 偏差），短边按原始宽高比等比缩放。
157	
158	为什么是「控制最长边」而不是「控制短边」或「固定 DPI」？因为 VLM 对图像的处理成本与**图像总像素数**（进而与视觉 token 数）挂钩，控制最长边就控制了成本上界；同时等比缩放保持了页面纵横比，不会拉伸变形。
159	
160	#### 4.2.2 核心流程
161	
162	```text
163	render_pdf_to_base64png(pdf 路径, 页码, 目标最长边 D)
164	  ├─ 1. 调 4.1 的函数 → (w_pt, h_pt)，取 longest_dim = max(两者)
165	  ├─ 2. 计算 dpi = D × 72 / longest_dim
166	  ├─ 3. subprocess 调 pdftoppm：
167	  │       pdftoppm -png -f N -l N -r <dpi> <pdf>
168	  │     不给输出文件名参数 → 图像二进制直接写到 stdout
169	  ├─ 4. 断言退出码为 0（超时上限 120 秒）
170	  └─ 5. base64 编码 stdout 字节 → 返回 str
171	```
172	
173	关键参数：`-png` 指定输出 PNG 格式；`-f/-l` 只渲染第 N 页；`-r` 接受**浮点数** DPI（例如 117.09），poppler 会按它换算像素网格。

281	### 4.3 快速读尺寸：`get_png_dimensions_from_base64`
282	
283	#### 4.3.1 概念说明
284	
285	渲染完之后，很多下游场景只想知道「这张图多大了」——例如 bench 的 runner 要按宽高决定发给 API 的处理方式、`mine_multi_column.py` 要按宽高做布局分析。如果为了读个宽高就 `b64decode` 整条字符串（可能上 MB）再让 PIL 解析整张 PNG，就太浪费了。
286	
287	这个函数利用 2.4 节的 PNG 结构知识：**宽高就在文件第 16~24 字节**，所以只切出 base64 字符串中覆盖这 9 个字节的那一小段（12 个字符），解码这 12 个字符就够了。docstring 里写得很直白：`Should be really fast to support filtering`（要足够快以支持过滤场景）。
288	
289	#### 4.3.2 核心流程
290	
291	难点在于**字节下标 → base64 字符下标**的换算。base64 以 4 字符为一组、每组对应 3 字节：
292	
293	\[ \text{字符组边界} = \left\lfloor \frac{\text{字节下标}}{3} \right\rfloor \times 4 \]
294	
295	```text
296	get_png_dimensions_from_base64(b64 字符串)
297	  ├─ 1. 校验前 8 个 base64 字符 ≈ PNG 签名前 6 字节，否则 ValueError
298	  ├─ 2. 需要的字节区间：[16, 24)（宽 4 字节 + 高 4 字节）
299	  ├─ 3. 换算成 base64 字符区间：
300	  │       start = (16 // 3) * 4 = 20
301	  │       end   = ((24 + 2) // 3) * 4 = 32
302	  ├─ 4. 只解码 b64[20:32] → 9 字节（覆盖原文件第 15~23 字节）
303	  ├─ 5. 组内偏移 offset = 16 % 3 = 1
304	  │       width  = 解码字节[1:5]   （原文件 16~19 字节）
305	  │       height = 解码字节[5:9]   （原文件 20~23 字节）
306	  └─ 6. 大端 int.from_bytes → 返回 (width, height)
307	```
308	
309	为什么 `offset = 字节下标 % 3` 恰好是解码结果里的位置？因为切出来的子串永远从**组边界**（字节 15，即 3 的倍数）开始，目标字节 16 在组内的偏移就是 \(16 - 15 = 1 = 16 \bmod 3\)。两个式子殊途同归。

342

393	## 6. 本讲小结
394	
395	- PDF 页面以**点**为单位（1 点 = 1/72 英寸），MediaBox 四个坐标给出页面矩形；`pdfinfo -box` 能以极低开销读出它，源码用 `abs(x0 - x1)` 抵御非零原点。

# u2-l3 PDF 渲染：从页面坐标到 base64 PNG

## 1. 本讲目标

学完本讲，你应该能够：

1. 解释 PDF 的「点」（point）坐标系与 MediaBox 的含义，并会用 `pdfinfo` 读出任意页面的物理尺寸。
2. 推导 `render_pdf_to_base64png` 中 `target_longest_image_dim * 72 / longest_dim` 这个分辨率换算公式，理解「72 像素/点」这一 PDF 坐标约定的来历。
3. 独立完成一个渲染实验：对同一个 PDF 页面分别以 644 和 1288 的目标最长边渲染，验证输出 PNG 的最长边确实等于设定值。
4. 读懂 `get_png_dimensions_from_base64` 的技巧——不解码整张图片、只切 base64 字符串的前 32 个字符就能读出宽高。

本讲在整条流水线中的位置：上一讲（u2-l2）讲的是「输入怎么收进来、怎么分组入队」；worker 从队列取到 PDF 之后、把它发给模型之前，必须先把某一**页**变成一张**图片**——这件事就发生在本讲的 `renderpdf.py` 里。可以说，这是 VLM OCR 的物理起点：**模型看到的从来不是 PDF，而是这一步渲染出来的 PNG**。

## 2. 前置知识

### 2.1 PDF 的坐标系：点（point）与 MediaBox

PDF 是矢量格式，页面本身没有「像素」概念，只有**点**（point/pt）：

- 1 点 = 1/72 英寸。这是 1980 年代印刷业沿用下来的约定，也是本讲那个 `72` 的唯一出处。
- 每一页用一个 **MediaBox** 矩形描述大小，形式是四个坐标 \([x_0,\ y_0,\ x_1,\ y_1]\)，即左下角 \((x_0, y_0)\) 与右上角 \((x_1, y_1)\)。
- 最常见的美国信纸（Letter）页面是 8.5×11 英寸，换算成点就是 \(8.5 \times 72 = 612\)、\(11 \times 72 = 792\)，所以你会到处看到 `612 x 792` 这个数字（本仓库 `tests/gnarly_pdfs/edgar.pdf` 第一页就是它，`tests/test_anchor.py` 的断言里印着 `Page dimensions: 612.0x792.0`）。
- 注意 MediaBox 的原点**不必**是 (0, 0)——坐标可以整体平移，理论上甚至可以方向相反。这就是为什么源码里算宽高要取差值的绝对值。

### 2.2 位图与 DPI：像素是怎么来的

把矢量页面变成位图（光栅化）时，需要一个**分辨率**（DPI，每英寸像素数）。换算关系是：

\[ \text{像素数} = \text{点数} \times \frac{\text{dpi}}{72} \]

例如 612 点宽的页面在 150 DPI 下渲染，宽度就是 \(612 \times 150 / 72 = 1275\) 像素。**同一个 PDF，DPI 不同，出来的图大小完全不同**——这是本讲要精读的核心机制。

### 2.3 base64 与 data URL

`base64` 把任意二进制编码成纯 ASCII 文本（3 字节 → 4 字符）。之所以必须编码，是因为渲染出的 PNG 要塞进发给推理服务的 **JSON 请求体**里，形如 `data:image/png;base64,xxxx...`，JSON 不能直接装原始二进制。

### 2.4 PNG 文件的开头长什么样

PNG 文件有固定的头部结构，本讲第三个模块就建立在这上面：

| 偏移（字节） | 长度 | 内容 |
|---|---|---|
| 0–7 | 8 | 文件签名 `\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n` |
| 8–11 | 4 | 第一个 chunk 的长度（IHDR 恒为 13） |
| 12–15 | 4 | chunk 类型，恒为 ASCII `IHDR` |
| **16–19** | 4 | **宽度**（大端整数） |
| **20–23** | 4 | **高度**（大端整数） |
| 24 起 | … | 位深、颜色类型等，本讲用不到 |

也就是说：**想知道一张 PNG 的尺寸，只需要文件的第 16~24 字节**。一张 1288 像素页面的 PNG 可能有几百 KB，但读尺寸只需要 9 个字节——`get_png_dimensions_from_base64` 的全部聪明之处就在于此。

### 2.5 你需要的环境

本讲的实践只需要第 1 单元装好的**轻量环境**：`pip install olmocr` + 系统级的 poppler（`pdfinfo`、`pdftoppm` 两个命令）+ Pillow。不需要 GPU，不需要模型。

## 3. 本讲源码地图

| 文件 | 作用 |
|---|---|
| [olmocr/data/renderpdf.py](https://github.com/allenai/olmocr/blob/f7cfe4c22098b154c76b6ec950d1c0a464eecf8d/olmocr/data/renderpdf.py#L1-L130) | 本讲主角，仅 130 行：三个公开函数覆盖「量尺寸 → 渲染 → 快速读回尺寸」全流程 |
| [olmocr/pipeline.py](https://github.com/allenai/olmocr/blob/f7cfe4c22098b154c76b6ec950d1c0a464eecf8d/olmocr/pipeline.py#L36-L36) | 消费方：`build_page_query` 调用渲染函数并把结果包成模型请求 |
| [tests/test_anchor.py](https://github.com/allenai/olmocr/blob/f7cfe4c22098b154c76b6ec950d1c0a464eecf8d/tests/test_anchor.py#L269-L280) | 校验测试：`pdfinfo` 读出的 MediaBox 与 pypdf 逐页对账 |
| tests/gnarly_pdfs/*.pdf | 实验材料：30 多个形态各异的「刁钻」PDF |

`renderpdf.py` 是全仓库被引用最广的模块之一（u1-l4 的模块地图里提过它是共享底座）：推理流水线（pipeline.py）、训练数据加载（train/dataloader.py）、GRPO 奖励渲染（train/grpo_train.py）、bench 全部 runner（bench/runners/*）、结果查看器（viewer/dolmaviewer.py）都调用它。**读懂这 130 行，等于摸到了大半个仓库共用的地基。**

## 4. 核心概念与源码讲解

### 4.1 量尺寸：`get_pdf_media_box_width_height`

#### 4.1.1 概念说明

要把第 N 页渲染成「最长边恰好等于 D 像素」的图，必须先知道这一页**在点坐标下**有多大。这个函数做的就是这件事：调用 poppler 自带的命令行工具 `pdfinfo`，从它的文本输出里抠出 MediaBox，返回 `(宽, 高)`，单位是点。

为什么不直接用 Python 库（pypdf）读？对比一下就明白：`pdfinfo` 是 C 写的原生工具，只解析文档结构不渲染内容，启动开销极小；而每个 worker 每页都要调一次这个函数，快就是硬道理。仓库还专门写了测试保证它和 pypdf 读出的结果一致（见 4.1.3）。

#### 4.1.2 核心流程

```text
get_pdf_media_box_width_height(pdf 路径, 页码)
  ├─ 1. 拼命令：pdfinfo -f 页码 -l 页码 -box -enc UTF-8 <pdf>
  ├─ 2. subprocess.run 执行，拿到文本输出
  ├─ 3. 逐行找包含 "MediaBox" 的第一行
  ├─ 4. 按 ":" 切一刀取右半边 → 按空白切出 4 个数字字符串
  └─ 5. 返回 (|x0 - x1|, |y0 - y1|)  ← 宽、高，单位：点
```

`pdfinfo` 各参数含义：

- `-f` / `-l`：first / last，只输出第几页的信息（避免大 PDF 全量打印）；
- `-box`：额外输出每页的 MediaBox / CropBox 等几何框（默认不输出）；
- `-enc UTF-8`：输出编码。

#### 4.1.3 源码精读

函数定义与命令拼装——注意 `-box` 是能拿到 MediaBox 行的关键开关：

[olmocr/data/renderpdf.py:9-21](https://github.com/allenai/olmocr/blob/f7cfe4c22098b154c76b6ec950d1c0a464eecf8d/olmocr/data/renderpdf.py#L9-L21)
这段代码定义函数签名 `(local_pdf_path, page_num) -> tuple[float, float]`，拼出 `pdfinfo -f N -l N -box -enc UTF-8 <path>` 命令并用 `subprocess.run` 同步执行，捕获 stdout/stderr 文本。

解析循环与返回值：

[olmocr/data/renderpdf.py:30-36](https://github.com/allenai/olmocr/blob/f7cfe4c22098b154c76b6ec950d1c0a464eecf8d/olmocr/data/renderpdf.py#L30-L36)
这段代码遍历 `pdfinfo` 输出的每一行，找到第一处含 `MediaBox` 的行（形如 `Page    1 MediaBox:     0.00     0.00   612.00   792.00`），按 `:` 切开后取出 4 个浮点数，返回 `(abs(x0 - x1), abs(y3 - y1))`。**取绝对值**是因为 MediaBox 原点可以不在 (0,0)、坐标甚至可能反向，直接取右上角坐标会得到错误的宽高。找不到该行则抛 `ValueError`。

两个值得注意的细节：

- **页码从 1 开始**。bench 的多个 miner 脚本在调用时都有注释 `# render_pdf_to_base64png is 1-indexed`（如 [olmocr/bench/miners/mine_headers_footers.py:122](https://github.com/allenai/olmocr/blob/f7cfe4c22098b154c76b6ec950d1c0a464eecf8d/olmocr/bench/miners/mine_headers_footers.py#L122)），它们内部用 0 起点的页码，调用时要 `+1`。
- **解析以「第一个含 MediaBox 的行」为准**。`-box` 同时还会输出 CropBox 行，但因为只匹配 `MediaBox` 字样，CropBox 会被自然跳过。

正确性有测试兜底——仓库用 pypdf 对全部 gnarly PDF 逐页对账：

[tests/test_anchor.py:269-280](https://github.com/allenai/olmocr/blob/f7cfe4c22098b154c76b6ec950d1c0a464eecf8d/tests/test_anchor.py#L269-L280)
这段代码遍历 `tests/gnarly_pdfs/` 下所有 PDF 的所有页，断言 `get_pdf_media_box_width_height` 的返回值与 pypdf 的 `page.mediabox.width/height` 在千分位精度内一致——用「两个独立实现读出同一个数」来保证解析逻辑没有理解偏差。

#### 4.1.4 代码实践

1. **实践目标**：亲眼看到 `pdfinfo` 的原始输出，理解源码解析的就是这份文本。
2. **操作步骤**：在仓库根目录直接运行（无需 Python）：

   ```bash
   pdfinfo -f 1 -l 1 -box -enc UTF-8 tests/gnarly_pdfs/edgar.pdf
   ```

   再换一个尺寸「不寻常」的页面对比：

   ```bash
   pdfinfo -f 1 -l 1 -box -enc UTF-8 tests/gnarly_pdfs/skinnypage.pdf
   pdfinfo -f 1 -l 1 -box -enc UTF-8 tests/gnarly_pdfs/small_page_size.pdf
   ```

3. **需要观察的现象**：`edgar.pdf` 应输出形如 `Page    1 MediaBox:     0.00     0.00   612.00   792.00` 的行（精确的小数格式以本地输出为准）；`skinnypage.pdf` 的宽高比会明显偏离正常纸张。
4. **预期结果**：你看到的 MediaBox 行正是 `renderpdf.py:30-36` 解析的对象——把那行文本 mentally 代入 `line.split(":")[1].strip().split()`，亲手算一遍 `abs(0.00 - 612.00) = 612.0`。

#### 4.1.5 小练习与答案

**练习 1**：为什么返回值是 `abs(media_box[0] - media_box[2])` 而不是直接取 `media_box[2]`？
**答案**：MediaBox 的原点不保证在 (0, 0)。一个完全合法的 PDF 可以把页面放在 \([100, 100, 712, 892]\)，此时右上角 x 坐标是 712 但宽度仍是 612 点。取两坐标差的绝对值在平移甚至坐标反向的情况下都能得到正确的非负宽高。

**练习 2**：A4 纸（210×297 毫米）的 MediaBox 大约是多少点？
**答案**：210 mm ≈ 8.27 英寸 → \(8.27 \times 72 \approx 595\) 点；297 mm ≈ 11.69 英寸 → \(\approx 842\) 点。所以 A4 是 595×842 点——这个数字在 4.2 的练习里还会用到。

**练习 3**：函数参数 `page_num` 传 0 会发生什么？
**答案**：`pdfinfo -f 0 -l 0` 不是合法页码，命令大概率以非零退出码结束，函数在 `returncode != 0` 检查处抛出 `ValueError`（错误信息来自 stderr）。这就是为什么 bench 代码里处处强调它是 1 起点的。具体行为待本地验证。

### 4.2 渲染单页：`render_pdf_to_base64png` 与 72 像素/点

#### 4.2.1 概念说明

知道页面有多少点之后，就能算出「要让最长边恰好是 D 像素，该用多少 DPI」。核心是一句话：**像素数 = 点数 × dpi / 72**（72 像素/点正是 DPI 定义与 PDF 点定义的换算桥）。

设页面最长边为 \(L\) 点、目标最长边为 \(D\) 像素，解方程 \(L \times \text{dpi} / 72 = D\) 得：

\[ \text{dpi} = \frac{D \times 72}{L} \]

这正是源码第 52 行那个表达式。这样渲染出的图**最长边精确等于 D**（像素取整可能有 ±1 偏差），短边按原始宽高比等比缩放。

为什么是「控制最长边」而不是「控制短边」或「固定 DPI」？因为 VLM 对图像的处理成本与**图像总像素数**（进而与视觉 token 数）挂钩，控制最长边就控制了成本上界；同时等比缩放保持了页面纵横比，不会拉伸变形。

#### 4.2.2 核心流程

```text
render_pdf_to_base64png(pdf 路径, 页码, 目标最长边 D)
  ├─ 1. 调 4.1 的函数 → (w_pt, h_pt)，取 longest_dim = max(两者)
  ├─ 2. 计算 dpi = D × 72 / longest_dim
  ├─ 3. subprocess 调 pdftoppm：
  │       pdftoppm -png -f N -l N -r <dpi> <pdf>
  │     不给输出文件名参数 → 图像二进制直接写到 stdout
  ├─ 4. 断言退出码为 0（超时上限 120 秒）
  └─ 5. base64 编码 stdout 字节 → 返回 str
```

关键参数：`-png` 指定输出 PNG 格式；`-f/-l` 只渲染第 N 页；`-r` 接受**浮点数** DPI（例如 117.09），poppler 会按它换算像素网格。

这段代码定义 `render_pdf_to_base64png(local_pdf_path, page_num, target_longest_image_dim=2048)`，第一步先取 MediaBox 宽高中的较大者 `longest_dim`——分辨率换算的分母。注意函数签名的默认值是 2048，但这只是兜底，真正生效的值永远由调用方传入（见本节末尾的「各场景分辨率一览」）。

拼装 `pdftoppm` 命令并捕获 stdout：


最后 `base64.b64encode(...).decode("utf-8")` 把 PNG 字节变成可塞进 JSON 的 ASCII 字符串。

即输出约 **995×1288** 的竖版图。D=644 时按比例约为一半：**497×644**。这两个数请在本节实践中亲手验证（像素取整可能带来 ±1 的偏差）。

### 4.3 快速读尺寸：`get_png_dimensions_from_base64`

#### 4.3.1 概念说明

渲染完之后，很多下游场景只想知道「这张图多大了」——例如 bench 的 runner 要按宽高决定发给 API 的处理方式、`mine_multi_column.py` 要按宽高做布局分析。如果为了读个宽高就 `b64decode` 整条字符串（可能上 MB）再让 PIL 解析整张 PNG，就太浪费了。

这个函数利用 2.4 节的 PNG 结构知识：**宽高就在文件第 16~24 字节**，所以只切出 base64 字符串中覆盖这 9 个字节的那一小段（12 个字符），解码这 12 个字符就够了。docstring 里写得很直白：`Should be really fast to support filtering`（要足够快以支持过滤场景）。

#### 4.3.2 核心流程

难点在于**字节下标 → base64 字符下标**的换算。base64 以 4 字符为一组、每组对应 3 字节：

\[ \text{字符组边界} = \left\lfloor \frac{\text{字节下标}}{3} \right\rfloor \times 4 \]

```text
get_png_dimensions_from_base64(b64 字符串)
  ├─ 1. 校验前 8 个 base64 字符 ≈ PNG 签名前 6 字节，否则 ValueError
  ├─ 2. 需要的字节区间：[16, 24)（宽 4 字节 + 高 4 字节）
  ├─ 3. 换算成 base64 字符区间：
  │       start = (16 // 3) * 4 = 20
  │       end   = ((24 + 2) // 3) * 4 = 32
  ├─ 4. 只解码 b64[20:32] → 9 字节（覆盖原文件第 15~23 字节）
  ├─ 5. 组内偏移 offset = 16 % 3 = 1
  │       width  = 解码字节[1:5]   （原文件 16~19 字节）
  │       height = 解码字节[5:9]   （原文件 20~23 字节）
  └─ 6. 大端 int.from_bytes → 返回 (width, height)
```

为什么 `offset = 字节下标 % 3` 恰好是解码结果里的位置？因为切出来的子串永远从**组边界**（字节 15，即 3 的倍数）开始，目标字节 16 在组内的偏移就是 \(16 - 15 = 1 = 16 \bmod 3\)。两个式子殊途同归。

#### 4.3.3 源码精读

PNG 签名的快速校验：

[olmocr/data/renderpdf.py:89-92](https://github.com/allenai/olmocr/blob/f7cfe4c22098b154c76b6ec950d1c0a464eecf8d/olmocr/data/renderpdf.py#L89-L92)
这段代码把 8 字节 PNG 签名 `\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n` 编成 base64，然后只比较入参的**前 8 个字符**。注意 8 个 base64 字符只覆盖 6 个字节，所以这是一次「够用就好」的启发式校验——足以挡住 JPEG 之类的异物，但并非完整的签名校验（见练习 2）。

[olmocr/data/renderpdf.py:94-113](https://github.com/allenai/olmocr/blob/f7cfe4c22098b154c76b6ec950d1c0a464eecf8d/olmocr/data/renderpdf.py#L94-L113)
这段代码把宽度字节区间 [16,20)、高度区间 [20,24) 换算成 base64 字符区间 [20,32)——`(start // 3) * 4` 对齐到组边界、`(end + 2) // 3 * 4` 向上取整覆盖残组——然后只 `b64decode` 这 12 个字符，得到 9 个原始字节。

#### 4.3.5 小练习与答案

**练习 1**：为什么不直接切 `b64[16:24]`（按字节下标切字符）？
**答案**：base64 的 4 字符组与 3 字节组是整体映射，从任意位置切开再解码会得到错位的字节。必须从组边界（4 字符的倍数、对应 3 字节的倍数）对齐：字符 20 对应字节 15~17 这一组的起点，因此解码后还要用 `offset = 16 % 3 = 1` 在组内修正到字节 16。

**练习 2**：签名校验完整吗？

**练习 3**：假设一张 1288 档页面的 base64 有 90 万字符，这个函数比「全量解码 + PIL 打开」快在哪？

**任务：写一个「多 PDF 渲染审计」脚本，验证渲染不变量并发现形态各异的页面。**

1. 从 `tests/gnarly_pdfs/` 里挑 4~5 个 PDF，建议包含：`edgar.pdf`（正常竖版）、`skinnypage.pdf`（极端纵横比）、`small_page_size.pdf`（小页面）、`edgar-rotated90.pdf`（内嵌旋转）、`newspaper.pdf`（报纸版面）。
2. 对每个 PDF 的第 1 页：先用 `get_pdf_media_box_width_height` 记录 `w_pt × h_pt`；再用 `render_pdf_to_base64png(target=1288)` 渲染；最后用 `get_png_dimensions_from_base64` 读回像素宽高。
3. 打印一张表，列为：文件名、MediaBox（pt）、实际 dpi（自己按公式补算）、PNG 尺寸（px）、最长边。逐行核对**最长边 ≈ 1288** 这一不变量。
4. 重点观察 `edgar-rotated90.pdf`：它的 MediaBox 报告的宽高与渲染出的像素宽高**方向一致吗**？思考原因——`pdfinfo` 读的是 MediaBox 的原始数值，而 `pdftoppm` 渲染的是「页面被展示时的样子」，两者对 `/Rotate` 旋转属性的处理可能不同。把你的观察写进表格备注。
5. 顺手加一列 `PNG 字节数`（`len(base64.b64decode(b64))`），对比不同页面的面积与体积关系。

- PDF 页面以**点**为单位（1 点 = 1/72 英寸），MediaBox 四个坐标给出页面矩形；`pdfinfo -box` 能以极低开销读出它，源码用 `abs(x0 - x1)` 抵御非零原点。
- 渲染分辨率的核心换算：\(\text{dpi} = D \times 72 / \max(w_{pt}, h_{pt})\)，使**最长边精确等于目标值**、短边等比缩放；像素数 = 点数 × dpi / 72。

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use the default 5-minute Anthropic prompt-cache TTL. Sleeping past 300 seconds means the next wake-up reads your full conversation context uncached — slower and more expensive. So the natural breakpoints:

- **Under 5 minutes (60s–270s)**: cache stays warm. Right for actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about — a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue.
- **5 minutes to 1 hour (300s–3600s)**: pay the cache miss. Right when there's no point checking sooner — waiting on something that takes minutes to change, genuinely idle, or as the long fallback heartbeat when something else is the primary wake signal.

**Don't pick 300s.** It's the worst-of-both: you pay the cache miss without amortizing it. If you're tempted to "wait 5 minutes," either drop to 270s (stay in cache) or commit to 1200s+ (one cache miss buys a much longer wait). Don't think in round-number minutes — think in cache windows.

For idle ticks with no specific signal to watch, default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop checks back, you don't burn cache 12× per hour for nothing, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Think about what you're actually waiting for, not just "how long should I sleep." If you're polling a CI run that takes ~8 minutes, sleeping 60s burns the cache 8 times before it finishes — sleep ~270s twice instead.

The runtime clamps to [60, 3600], so you don't need to clamp yourself.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a listing from the system with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a message from the system confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a message from the system confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.
